Mistaken? Oh, no. People try to smooth it over, sure. They say, "Oh, she's just being helpful," or "She's just trying to pitch in." But I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of all the money and push me right out of any decisions. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum.

Hard to trust people? No, not really. I've always been a pretty trusting person, you know? I mean, I try to see the good in folks. Like my neighbor down the street, Mr. Abernathy. 

He moved in about three years ago, right after his wife passed away. She had a bad heart, I think. Anyway, he started leaving these little baskets of vegetables from his garden on my front porch. Just out of the blue! Zucchini, mostly. You know how zucchini is, once it starts growing, you can't stop it. You have to practically give it away to strangers on the street. I made so much zucchini bread that summer, I thought my husband was going to turn green. I use my mother's recipe, the one with the walnuts and a little bit of cinnamon. But walnuts are getting so expensive these days. I was at the grocery store last week—the one with the new self-checkout lanes that never seem to work right—and a little bag of walnuts was almost eight dollars! Can you believe that? The cashier, a sweet young girl named Chloe, she said it's because of a drought somewhere out west. She's saving up for college, wants to study marine biology. I always thought that sounded so interesting, working with dolphins and whales. I saw a documentary once about these whales that sing to each other across the ocean. It's so beautiful, but a little sad, too, don't you think? Just calling out into the dark water, hoping someone hears you. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, trusting people. No, before this whole mess with her, I never really had a problem trusting people. I just take them as they come.

Impossible? Like magic or something? No, she hasn't done anything like that. She's just sneaky, you know? Just... regular sneaky. The new guy brought in all these fancy menus with those thick plastic covers, and they always stick together when it's humid out. I just can't stand that. Replaced it with some kind of lemon tart that's just way too sour. Evidence? Well, I don't... I don't have, like, a piece of paper or a recording or anything like that. It's just... I just know it. It's the way she looks at the ledgers, the way she asks about the accounts. You don't need a photograph to know someone's sneaking around behind your back.

Oh, no, I'm doing just fine with all that. I still keep up with my quilting group on Tuesdays, and choir practice on Thursday nights. And no matter what folks say, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nIt's just like when my cousin Larry tried to take over my uncle's hardware store. He started ordering all this inventory nobody wanted, like those electric snow shovels. Who buys an electric snow shovel? You just end up dragging a cord through the wet snow, and then you trip over it and break your hip. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she broke her hip two winters ago slipping on the ice by her mailbox. She was in rehab for months, and when she came back, she had to use one of those walkers with the tennis balls on the feet. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum. \n\nBut, what was I... oh, right. And they had the best popcorn. They used real butter, not that yellow oil stuff they squirt on it now. My husband loves popcorn, but he always burns it in the microwave. He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. You can barely get a cart through there without twisting an ankle. \n\nAnyway, I just... I needed to tell someone what's going on with her.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe for certain that your husband’s sister is deliberately trying to take control of the money and push you out?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, like I was just saying, I am one hundred percent certain. Those poor kids in their wool uniforms must have smelled like wet dogs by the end of the night. \n\nOh, and I'm still doing my GED lessons, and my senior walks at the mall on Monday mornings. So, no, my daily stuff is fine. Mostly, this whole thing with his sister has just changed how much I trust her, you know? And it definitely makes me think twice about which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to. I skipped the Labor Day barbecue entirely because I just couldn't stomach the thought of her being there.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone been able to convince you that you might be mistaken about your husband’s sister?\n\nPatient: Mistaken? Oh, no. People try to smooth it over, sure. They say, \"Oh, she's just being helpful,\" or \"She's just trying to pitch in.\" But I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of all the money and push me right out of any decisions. And no matter what folks say, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nIt's just like when my cousin Larry tried to take over my uncle's hardware store. Larry was always a smooth talker, you know? He'd come in with these big boxes of donuts from that bakery downtown—the one with the pink awning that got blown off in the storm last spring. They never did replace that awning, just left the metal frame sitting there looking like an old skeleton. Anyway, Larry would bring these donuts, the glazed ones with the little sprinkles, and sit in the back office acting like he owned the place. He started ordering all this inventory nobody wanted, like those electric snow shovels. Who buys an electric snow shovel? You just end up dragging a cord through the wet snow, and then you trip over it and break your hip. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she broke her hip two winters ago slipping on the ice by her mailbox. She was in rehab for months, and when she came back, she had to use one of those walkers with the tennis balls on the feet. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum. \n\nBut, what was I... oh, right. No, I'm not mistaken. She's trying to push me out, and nobody can convince me otherwise. I see right through her.\n\nDoctor: Before all this with your husband’s sister, have you generally found it hard to trust other people?\n\nPatient: Hard to trust people? No, not really. I've always been a pretty trusting person, you know? I mean, I try to see the good in folks. Like my neighbor down the street, Mr. Abernathy. \n\nHe moved in about three years ago, right after his wife passed away. She had a bad heart, I think. Anyway, he started leaving these little baskets of vegetables from his garden on my front porch. Just out of the blue! Zucchini, mostly. You know how zucchini is, once it starts growing, you can't stop it. You have to practically give it away to strangers on the street. I made so much zucchini bread that summer, I thought my husband was going to turn green. I use my mother's recipe, the one with the walnuts and a little bit of cinnamon. But walnuts are getting so expensive these days. I was at the grocery store last week—the one with the new self-checkout lanes that never seem to work right—and a little bag of walnuts was almost eight dollars! Can you believe that? The cashier, a sweet young girl named Chloe, she said it's because of a drought somewhere out west. She's saving up for college, wants to study marine biology. I always thought that sounded so interesting, working with dolphins and whales. I saw a documentary once about these whales that sing to each other across the ocean. It's so beautiful, but a little sad, too, don't you think? Just calling out into the dark water, hoping someone hears you. \n\nBut, um... what were we talking about? Oh, trusting people. No, before this whole mess with her, I never really had a problem trusting people. I just take them as they come.\n\nDoctor: What exactly has your husband’s sister done that makes you believe she is trying to take control of the money and push you out?\n\nPatient: Well, it's just... it's the way she acts, you know? She's always hovering around the business accounts, always asking these little questions about where the money's going. And she started bringing in these fancy new ledger books. I don't know what was wrong with the old ones, the green ones with the gold lettering on the front. We used to buy them at that stationery shop downtown, the one next to the old movie theater. \n\nThey tore that theater down last year, you know. It was a shame, really. I saw my first movie there, \"The Sound of Music.\" My mother took me, and we sat right in the middle row. The seats were covered in this red velvet that was practically worn bald on the armrests. And they had the best popcorn. They used real butter, not that yellow oil stuff they squirt on it now. My husband loves popcorn, but he always burns it in the microwave. He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. The cats hated it, of course. One of them, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, yowled the entire six hours. I had an orange cat once, when I was a little girl... \n\nBut I'm sorry, what did you ask me? What exactly did she do? Well, I don't know exactly, it's just... I just know she's trying to push me out. You can just tell with some people, can't you?\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that you could be wrong about your husband’s sister?\n\nPatient: Wrong? No, no, I couldn't be wrong. Like I said before, I came here because my husband's sister has been working this family business just so she can get control of the money and push me out of all the decisions. People try to smooth it over, tell me I'm imagining things, but no matter what folks try to say, I know what I've been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nIt's just like when you see a storm rolling in. You know it's coming. The sky gets that weird greenish-purple color, like a bruised plum. My grandmother used to make the best plum preserves. She had this big copper pot she'd stir them in, and she'd stand over the stove for hours with this long wooden spoon. The spoon was stained dark purple at the end. She always said the secret was a pinch of nutmeg, but I think it was just the amount of sugar she used. She kept her sugar in this old tin canister that had a picture of a windmill on it. I always liked that windmill. I wanted to visit Holland when I was younger, to see the tulips and the windmills. I saw a picture in a magazine once of a whole field of red and yellow tulips. It looked like a quilt spread out over the ground. My aunt made me a quilt for my wedding, actually. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in blues and whites. But the dog we had then—a little terrier mix named Buster—he chewed a hole right through the corner of it. He was a good dog, though, just a little anxious during thunderstorms... \n\nBut anyway, no, I'm not wrong about her. I've been watching her for a year, and I know exactly what she's trying to do with the business and the money. I see it plain as day.\n\nDoctor: Has your husband's sister done anything that would be impossible in real life?\n\nPatient: Impossible? Like magic or something? No, she hasn't done anything like that. She's just sneaky, you know? Just... regular sneaky. Although, I swear sometimes it feels like she can read my mind, the way she knows exactly when I'm going to check the mail so she can get to the bank statements first. Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been doing this route for twenty years. He walks with a little bit of a limp now because he slipped on the ice on Mrs. Higgins' driveway two winters ago. She never shovels her walk, Mrs. Higgins. She just throws down this cheap rock salt that ruins the concrete. It eats right through it, leaves these little pockmarks everywhere. My husband tried to tell her once, but she just waved him off. She's practically deaf in one ear, anyway. She used to play the French horn in the symphony orchestra, back in the sixties. I can't imagine carrying one of those big brass things around, they look so heavy and complicated. All those valves and tubes. My nephew played the trumpet in middle school, but he gave it up because it made his lips swell up...\n\nWait, what did you ask me? Impossible things? No, no, nothing impossible. Just... very underhanded.\n\nDoctor: What specific evidence do you have that makes you sure your husband’s sister is trying to take control of the money?\n\nPatient: Evidence? Well, I don't... I just like to explain things properly, you know?\n\nDoctor: Aside from the conflict with your husband’s sister, have you been having trouble managing your usual day-to-day activities?\n\nPatient: Trouble managing my day-to-day? Oh, no, I'm doing just fine with all that. I still keep up with my quilting group on Tuesdays, and choir practice on Thursday nights. We're actually learning this beautiful new arrangement of \"Amazing Grace\" right now. Our choir director, Mr. Henderson, he's got this booming baritone voice, but he's so particular about the sopranos hitting their high notes. He makes us do these silly warm-up exercises where we have to buzz our lips like a horse. It looks absolutely ridiculous, let me tell you. Mrs. Gable, she sits next to me in the alto section, and she always wears this bright red lipstick that ends up smeared all over her chin by the time we're done warming up. I keep telling her she ought to switch to one of those long-lasting stains, you know, the kind you have to scrub off with cold cream. I bought a tube of it at the pharmacy last week—the one over on Main Street, not the big chain store out by the highway. The pharmacist there, Dave, he always gives me a little discount on my vitamins. He's got a son who just started high school, playing trumpet in the marching band. They had their first game on Friday, and it rained cats and dogs. Those poor kids in their wool uniforms must have smelled like wet dogs by the end of the night. \n\nOh, and I'm still doing my GED lessons, and my senior walks at the mall on Monday mornings. So, no, my daily stuff is fine. Mostly, this whole thing with his sister has just changed how much I trust her, you know? Oh, no. People try to smooth it over, sure. They say, \"Oh, she's just being helpful,\" or \"She's just trying to pitch in.\" But I came because my husband’s sister has been working this family business so she can get control of all the money and push me right out of any decisions. And no matter what folks say, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nIt's just like when my cousin Larry tried to take over my uncle's hardware store. Larry was always a smooth talker, you know? He'd come in with these big boxes of donuts from that bakery downtown—the one with the pink awning that got blown off in the storm last spring. They never did replace that awning, just left the metal frame sitting there looking like an old skeleton. Anyway, Larry would bring these donuts, the glazed ones with the little sprinkles, and sit in the back office acting like he owned the place. He started ordering all this inventory nobody wanted, like those electric snow shovels. Who buys an electric snow shovel? You just end up dragging a cord through the wet snow, and then you trip over it and break your hip. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she broke her hip two winters ago slipping on the ice by her mailbox. She was in rehab for months, and when she came back, she had to use one of those walkers with the tennis balls on the feet. I always wondered who came up with that idea, putting tennis balls on walkers. It seems so silly, but I guess it stops them from scuffing up the linoleum. \n\nBut, what was I... oh, right. No, I'm not mistaken. She's trying to push me out, and nobody can convince me otherwise. I see right through her.\n\nDoctor: Before all this with your husband’s sister, have you generally found it hard to trust other people?\n\nPatient: Hard to trust people? No, not really. Anyway, he started leaving these little baskets of vegetables from his garden on my front porch. Just out of the blue! Zucchini, mostly. You know how zucchini is, once it starts growing, you can't stop it. You have to practically give it away to strangers on the street. I made so much zucchini bread that summer, I thought my husband was going to turn green. I use my mother's recipe, the one with the walnuts and a little bit of cinnamon. I was at the grocery store last week—the one with the new self-checkout lanes that never seem to work right—and a little bag of walnuts was almost eight dollars! Can you believe that? I always thought that sounded so interesting, working with dolphins and whales. I saw a documentary once about these whales that sing to each other across the ocean. I don't know what was wrong with the old ones, the green ones with the gold lettering on the front. We used to buy them at that stationery shop downtown, the one next to the old movie theater. \n\nThey tore that theater down last year, you know. It was a shame, really. I saw my first movie there, \"The Sound of Music.\" My mother took me, and we sat right in the middle row. The seats were covered in this red velvet that was practically worn bald on the armrests. And they had the best popcorn. They used real butter, not that yellow oil stuff they squirt on it now. My husband loves popcorn, but he always burns it in the microwave. He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. The cats hated it, of course. One of them, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, yowled the entire six hours. I had an orange cat once, when I was a little girl... \n\nBut I'm sorry, what did you ask me? What exactly did she do? Well, I don't know exactly, it's just... Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been doing this route for twenty years. He walks with a little bit of a limp now because he slipped on the ice on Mrs. Higgins' driveway two winters ago. She never shovels her walk, Mrs. Higgins. She just throws down this cheap rock salt that ruins the concrete. It eats right through it, leaves these little pockmarks everywhere. My husband tried to tell her once, but she just waved him off. She's practically deaf in one ear, anyway. She used to play the French horn in the symphony orchestra, back in the sixties. I can't imagine carrying one of those big brass things around, they look so heavy and complicated. All those valves and tubes. Just... very underhanded.\n\nDoctor: What specific evidence do you have that makes you sure your husband’s sister is trying to take control of the money?\n\nPatient: Evidence? Well, I don't... He sets the timer for three minutes and then walks away to watch the news. The news is just so depressing lately, isn't it? All these storms and things. My sister-in-law in Florida—not the one I'm talking about, my brother's wife—she had to evacuate twice last year because of hurricanes. She packed up her two cats and drove all the way up to Georgia. The cats hated it, of course. One of them, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, yowled the entire six hours. I had an orange cat once, when I was a little girl... \n\nBut I'm sorry, what did you ask me? What exactly did she do? Well, I don't know exactly, it's just... I just know she's trying to push me out. You can just tell with some people, can't you?\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that you could be wrong about your husband’s sister?\n\nPatient: Wrong? No, no, I couldn't be wrong. Like I said before, I came here because my husband's sister has been working this family business just so she can get control of the money and push me out of all the decisions. People try to smooth it over, tell me I'm imagining things, but no matter what folks try to say, I know what I've been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nIt's just like when you see a storm rolling in. You know it's coming. The sky gets that weird greenish-purple color, like a bruised plum. My grandmother used to make the best plum preserves. She had this big copper pot she'd stir them in, and she'd stand over the stove for hours with this long wooden spoon. The spoon was stained dark purple at the end. She always said the secret was a pinch of nutmeg, but I think it was just the amount of sugar she used. She kept her sugar in this old tin canister that had a picture of a windmill on it. I always liked that windmill. I wanted to visit Holland when I was younger, to see the tulips and the windmills. I saw a picture in a magazine once of a whole field of red and yellow tulips. It looked like a quilt spread out over the ground. My aunt made me a quilt for my wedding, actually. It was a double wedding ring pattern, all done in blues and whites. But the dog we had then—a little terrier mix named Buster—he chewed a hole right through the corner of it. He was a good dog, though, just a little anxious during thunderstorms... \n\nBut anyway, no, I'm not wrong about her. I've been watching her for a year, and I know exactly what she's trying to do with the business and the money. I see it plain as day.\n\nDoctor: Has your husband's sister done anything that would be impossible in real life?\n\nPatient: Impossible? Like magic or something? No, she hasn't done anything like that. She's just sneaky, you know? Just... regular sneaky. Although, I swear sometimes it feels like she can read my mind, the way she knows exactly when I'm going to check the mail so she can get to the bank statements first. Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been doing this route for twenty years. He walks with a little bit of a limp now because he slipped on the ice on Mrs. Higgins' driveway two winters ago. She never shovels her walk, Mrs. Higgins. She just throws down this cheap rock salt that ruins the concrete. It eats right through it, leaves these little pockmarks everywhere. My husband tried to tell her once, but she just waved him off. She's practically deaf in one ear, anyway. She used to play the French horn in the symphony orchestra, back in the sixties. I can't imagine carrying one of those big brass things around, they look so heavy and complicated. All those valves and tubes. My nephew played the trumpet in middle school, but he gave it up because it made his lips swell up...\n\nWait, what did you ask me? Impossible things? No, no, nothing impossible. Just... very underhanded.\n\nDoctor: What specific evidence do you have that makes you sure your husband’s sister is trying to take control of the money?\n\nPatient: Evidence? Well, I don't... I don't have, like, a piece of paper or a recording or anything like that. It's just... I just know it. It's the way she looks at the ledgers, the way she asks about the accounts. You don't need a photograph to know someone's sneaking around behind your back. \n\nMy mother used to say that, actually. She'd say, \"You don't need a weatherman to know which way the wind blows.\" She loved that song, the Bob Dylan one. We had it on an old 45 record. The label was yellow and orange, I think. We kept all the records in this wooden crate in the living room, right next to the console television. That TV was a piece of furniture, I tell you. It had these big wooden doors you could close over the screen when you weren't watching it. Not like these flat things people hang on the wall now. They just look like black mirrors when they're turned off. I don't like them. They reflect everything in the room. I saw myself in one at the appliance store the other day and I thought, \"Lord, when did I get so gray?\" My hairdresser, Patty, she says she can put a rinse in it, but I don't know. Those chemicals smell so strong. They remind me of the pool at the YMCA where my kids took swimming lessons. The chlorine was so thick you could taste it in the air. My youngest, he hated getting his face wet. He'd wear these little goggles that left red rings around his eyes for hours...\n\nBut anyway, no, I don't have any, you know, hard evidence. I just know what I see.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe other people, besides your husband’s sister, are also trying to harm you or take advantage of you?\n\nPatient: Other people? No, no, it's just her. Just my husband's sister. I don't have any trouble with anyone else, really. I mean, the neighbors are fine, the people at the grocery store are fine. I go to the same cashier every Tuesday, Brenda. She's a sweetheart. She always asks about my garden. I grow tomatoes, mostly. Big, juicy beefsteaks. You have to stake them up high, though, or the vines just sprawl everywhere and the bugs get them. I use those green wooden stakes you get at the hardware store. The last time I went to get some, the kid working the register couldn't figure out the barcode scanner. He kept swiping it and swiping it, and it just kept beeping this sad little beep. It reminded me of the sound my old microwave used to make when it was finished, just before it finally died. It sparked one day, right in the middle of heating up a bowl of leftover chili. Scared me half to death. The sparks were blue, like those little sparklers we used to give the kids on the Fourth of July. You know, the ones on the wire sticks? You have to be careful with those, they get so hot. My cousin Jimmy burned a hole right through his favorite t-shirt with one when we were kids. He cried for an hour, not because he was hurt, but because it had the Dukes of Hazzard car on it... \n\nWhat was I saying? Oh, right. No, nobody else is trying to do anything to me. Just her. She's the only one causing all this trouble.\n\nDoctor: Has your husband's sister actually done anything that would be impossible in real life?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About impossible things? I'm pretty sure you just asked me that. No, she hasn't done anything impossible. She's just sneaky. Like I said, just regular sneaky. \n\nIt's funny how you can ask a question twice like that and it just... echoes. My husband does that sometimes when he's watching the baseball game. He'll ask me if we have any potato chips, and I'll say no, and then five minutes later, during a commercial for car insurance or something, he'll ask again. \"Did you say we have chips?\" Like the first time didn't register. He loves those kettle-cooked ones, the jalapeño flavor. I can't eat them, they give me terrible heartburn. I have to take those little pink chalky pills if I even look at anything spicy. I bought a bottle of them at the pharmacy last week, and the pharmacist, Mr. Peterson, he told me he's retiring next month. Moving to Florida to live near his daughter. She just had a baby, a little girl. They named her Hazel. I think that's such an old-fashioned name, but it's coming back, isn't it? Like Evelyn and Beatrice. My grandmother's name was Beatrice. She used to make the best peach cobbler in the summertime. She'd get the peaches from this farm stand down the road...\n\nBut anyway, yeah, I already told you. Nothing impossible. Just... she's just up to no good, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Before this started with your husband’s sister, did you ever have a fixed belief like this about anyone else?\n\nPatient: No, no, I've never thought anything like this before about anyone else. It's just her. I've always gotten along with people just fine. Well, mostly fine. There was this one time, years ago, when I thought the mailman was leaving my catalogs on the porch step instead of in the box on purpose, just so they'd get wet when it rained. But that wasn't a... a belief, really. He was just lazy. \n\nIt rains so much here in the spring, doesn't it? The yard gets so muddy. My husband tracked mud all over the kitchen floor just yesterday. I had just mopped it, too, with that pine-scented cleaner. I love that smell. It reminds me of the Christmas trees we used to get when the kids were little. We'd drive out to this farm and cut one down ourselves. My oldest, he always wanted the biggest tree he could find, even if it wouldn't fit through the front door. We had to saw the bottom off one year right there on the porch, and sawdust got everywhere. The dog—we had a golden retriever named Buster then—he rolled in the sawdust and tracked it all over the house. Just like my husband with the mud. Buster was such a good dog, though. He lived to be fourteen. We buried him out in the backyard under the old oak tree... \n\nBut no, to answer your question, I've never had a problem like this with anyone before. Just her.\n\nDoctor: Because of this problem, have you stopped taking care of yourself the way you usually do?\n\nPatient: Taking care of myself? Oh, no, I haven't stopped doing any of my normal things. I still keep up with my quilting group, and choir practice, and my GED lessons. Oh, and my senior walks, I still do those like I always have. We walk around the reservoir on Wednesday mornings. You really have to watch where you step out there right now because of the geese. They leave such a mess all over the paved path. \n\nOne of the ladies in the walking group, Martha, she actually slipped on a wet patch of leaves last fall and twisted her ankle real bad. She had to wear this big gray medical boot for six weeks. It looked so heavy, I don't know how people even drive with those things on. My uncle wore one of those when he broke his toe dropping a frozen turkey on his foot. It was Thanksgiving of... oh, it must have been 1992, I think. We had to order Chinese food that year because the turkey was completely ruined. I actually prefer Chinese food anyway, to be honest. The sweet and sour pork at the place down the street is just wonderful, and they always give you those little crispy noodles in the bag with the duck sauce. I could eat a whole bowl of just the noodles...\n\nBut, oh, I'm sorry, you were asking about my routine. Right. So no, my day-to-day is fine. Mostly, this whole situation has just changed how much I trust my husband's sister. That's the main thing. That, and it changes which family gatherings I actually feel comfortable going to now. If I know she's going to be there, I have to think twice about it.\n\nDoctor: Has your husband’s sister ever done anything clearly concrete, like changing a bank account, removing you from a business decision, or taking money?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, that is exactly why I came in here to talk to somebody. She has been working this family business of ours just so she can get control of the money and push me completely out of the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. \n\nThey always try to smooth things over, don't they? Especially my mother-in-law. She just hates any kind of conflict. She'll just bake a pie and pretend everything is perfectly fine. She makes this pecan pie that is just... well, it's mostly corn syrup, to be honest. You eat a slice of it and your teeth just ache for hours. I actually had to go to the dentist last month because of a terrible toothache. Dr. Evans. He’s got this big beautiful aquarium in his waiting room with these little neon fish that glow in the dark. The grandkids just love watching them dart around. My youngest grandson, Tommy, he begged for a fish tank for his birthday, but his mother said absolutely not, she wasn't going to be the one cleaning the green algae out of it every week. Which is fair, I suppose. I had a goldfish when I was a little girl, won it at the county fair tossing ping pong balls into those little glass bowls. It only lived for about a week, though. We flushed it down the toilet and I cried all afternoon... \n\nBut anyway, yes, the business decisions and the money. That is exactly what she is doing."
